themes.tagline: Three videos walk into a bar — and none of them can agree on why they can't walk back out.

items.title: Why Does Time Only Go One Way?
items.description:
Head to https://squarespace.com/physicsexplained to save 10% off your first purchase of a website or domain using code PHYSICSEXPLAINED

Why does time only go one way? Why do broken things never unbreak, and why does the universe remember the past but not the future? The laws of physics work just as well forwards as backwards in time—so where does the arrow of time really come from?

In this video, we follow entropy from simple coin tosses and mixing gases all the way to black holes and the Big
items.why_watch: This 42-minute deep dive earns its runtime by carefully building from thermodynamic basics to the real puzzle: the laws of physics are time-symmetric, so the arrow of time must come from somewhere else entirely — specifically, the improbably low-entropy initial conditions of the universe. It's one of the cleaner explanations of why the past hypothesis matters without requiring any prior physics background.

items.why_watch: The video's core argument — that entropy is fundamentally a mathematical counting problem about accessible microstates, not a physical tendency toward "disorder" — reframes a concept most people learned incorrectly in school. The payoff is a clearer, less hand-wavy explanation of why time's arrow exists that doesn't rely on intuition-pumping analogies.

items.title: Einstein's Relativity contains a HUGE Loophole. Its Implications Can't Be Ignored.
items.description:
An extraordinary misunderstanding lies at the heart of relativity, born in the overlooked distinction between the empirical verifiability of the two-way speed of light and the presumed isotropy of one-way light speed. What is this distinction exactly, and how might making it explicit shake the foundations of our entire paradigm of modern physics?

Thank you for watching and please consider supporting us on Patreon! https://www.patreon.com/dialect_philosophy


References and Sources:

Einstein, A
items.why_watch: The specific loophole explored here is the one-way vs. two-way speed of light distinction: we've only ever measured light speed on a round trip, which means the assumption that light travels at the same speed in all directions is a convention, not an experimental fact. The video is careful not to overclaim, making it a genuinely thought-provoking look at what relativity actually proves versus what it assumes.

themes.name: The Slow Collapse
themes.tagline: When a brand that seemed immortal quietly starts falling apart — and the business decisions that got it there.

items.title: Is 7-Eleven In Trouble?
items.description:
Since its founding in 1927, the convenience store 7-Eleven has become an iconic part of American life, famous for its Slurpees and Big Gulps, being open 24/7 as well as the promise that no matter where you were, there was always one nearby. But recently, something feels different: there are fewer 7-Elevens than you remember. So what happened?

In this episode of Weird History, we’re digging into the strange history of 7-Eleven to explain how a small icehouse became one of the world’s most recogn
items.why_watch: 7-Eleven has quietly been closing stores at a notable rate, and this video traces the specific business decisions — from its Japanese parent company Ito-Yokado to the failed 2024 acquisition bid — that explain the decline. It's a tidy 14-minute retail autopsy that connects convenience store economics to broader shifts in how Americans actually shop now.

morning_soundtrack.title: Lala Lala Shares Surprise Piano Album Wall Tongue
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Earlier this year, Lillie West released the latest Lala Lala record, Heaven 2 . The nomadic indie artist likes to go on side quests; in 2024 she shared an instrumental album called if i were a real man i would be able to break the neck of a suffering bird . Now, she's back with a surprise piano LP called Wall Tongue .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Quiet, introspective keystrokes echoing through an empty apartment at 2am, when words feel too heavy to carry.

Today marks the 40th anniversary of the band's final live performance in Spain. To commemorate, we're pleased to share an edited extract from In Another World.

global_silver_linings.title: Researchers Use Math to Ensure a Wordle Win 99% of the Time
global_silver_linings.snippet: Millions of people playing their daily Wordle games will be eager to hear about this new research. Using information theory, the team of researchers from Binghamton University and State University of New York has developed a method to solve the game with a 99% success rate. In the The New York Times online game, players […]
global_silver_linings.reason: It's quietly delightful that mathematicians are turning their skills toward something as joyful and communal as a daily word game. A reminder that serious tools can serve simple, human pleasures.

global_silver_linings.title: Hospice nurse reveals the exact time people are most likely to die and it’s fascinating
global_silver_linings.reason: Hospice nurses carry some of life's hardest knowledge, and when they share it openly, it helps the rest of us approach death with less fear and more understanding — a genuine gift to anyone facing loss.

featured_read.title: Gondwana Really Was a Supercontinent
featured_read.snippet: And it helped kick‑start life on Earth
featured_read.blurb: Before continents were landmarks, they were engines — and Gondwana, it turns out, may have been the engine that got life itself moving. This piece traces how a single ancient landmass quietly set the table for everything that followed.

reading_room.title: Lessons from Wyatt Earp country
reading_room.snippet: How does a man show up for his community? I learned from an old farmer on the edge of the desert - by Zeno Franco Read on Psyche
reading_room.blurb: On the edge of Wyatt Earp country, a writer meets an old farmer and finds an unexpectedly quiet answer to a question men rarely ask aloud: what does it actually mean to show up? Bring your patience for the kind of wisdom that doesn't announce itself.

reading_room.title: The Extraordinary Untold Story of Freddie Mercury: Mary Austin on Her Best Friend–and Love of Her Life
reading_room.snippet: "He was Queen’s flamboyant frontman. She was his shy girlfriend, dreaming of marriage until they both realised he preferred men."
reading_room.blurb: Mary Austin watched Freddie Mercury become a legend while quietly holding the part of him the world never saw — and this is her account of a love that didn't fit any category either of them had a name for. It's a portrait of devotion in the negative space of fame.

reading_room.title: Lit Hub Daily: September 11, 2026
reading_room.snippet: Where does Harlan Coben get ideas? “Sometimes, it’s a simple ‘what-if.’” | Lit Hub Craft Phillip Lopate explores the lore and legacy of “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.” | Lit Hub Biography Steven W. Thrasher reads No God But Us
reading_room.blurb: A roundup rather than a single essay, today's Lit Hub daily skips the longread invitation — but Phillip Lopate on the gothic fog of Sleepy Hollow is worth the detour if you have ten spare minutes.

reading_room.title: The Property-Tax Revolution
reading_room.blurb: Property-tax cuts feel like relief until they become a slow structural collapse — this piece maps exactly how states are quietly sawing off the branch they're sitting on. The fiscal sleight-of-hand is more alarming, and more intimate, than the dry headline suggests.

reading_room.title: Facing the Music
reading_room.blurb: A poem named 'Facing the Music' is already asking you to sit with something you've been putting off — set aside two minutes and let it ask the question properly.
